findings.title: A live but unrelated PID in the pid file now blocks every reconnect
findings.body: The script now treats any `REMOTE_PID` that passes `server_running` (`kill -0` and not a zombie, lines 625-630) as our own busy server. If `wait_ready` fails, it exits 1 and leaves `pid`/`port`/`managed` in place (lines 720-722). Picture this: the remote host reboots, or the server crashes and gets reaped by init, and later another process takes that PID. `resolve_default_runtime_port` also only does `process.kill(pid, 0)` (line 650). So the stale runtime file still matches `REMOTE_PID`, the check at line 671 sends the run down this branch, and every connection attempt waits 60s and then prints "the server was left running. Retry the connection". A retry ends the same way, and the client never recovers on its own. Before this change, the 2s probe failing made the script relaunch. The only ways out now are a runner update or a disconnect. Both end up sending SIGTERM to the unrelated process (lines 715, 780-781). If that process ignores SIGTERM, the stop script keeps the files (lines 787-789) and the user stays stuck. Suggestion: before trusting the PID, check that it is our server, e.g. `ps -o args= -p "$REMOTE_PID"` contains `$RUNNER_FILE` or `serve`. When it doesn't match, fall through to the relaunch branch.

findings.title: An interrupt between delete and close leaks the stale SSH forward
findings.body: `tunnels.delete(key)` now runs before `closeTunnelEntry(entry)`, and nothing makes the pair uninterruptible. If the `ensureEnvironment` fiber is interrupted after the delete but before `Scope.close` (line 1392), the entry's scope is never closed. That scope is a standalone `Scope.make` (line 1558), and the manager finalizer only closes entries still in `tunnels` (lines 1401-1408), so the `ssh -N` process stays alive until the app exits. `disconnectEnvironment` does the same delete-then-close inside `Effect.uninterruptible` (lines 1782-1785). Wrapping this pair the same way closes the gap.

contracts.action: Replace a stale local SSH forward without running the remote stop
contracts.equivalent_path: disconnectEnvironment deletes the entry, then closes it (tunnel.ts:1782-1785)
contracts.before_after: The entry finalizer runs stopRemoteServer only when tunnels.get(key) === entry (tunnel.ts:1587-1597). Deleting first makes the stale-forward close kill only the local ssh process. createTunnelEntry then reruns the launch script, which reuses the running server.
contracts.visible_effect: On reconnect, the remote server and its agents keep running. The client gets a new forward to the same remote port.
contracts.failure_mode: If interrupted between delete and close, the entry scope (tunnel.ts:1558) is never closed, and the manager finalizer (tunnel.ts:1401-1408) can no longer see the entry, so the ssh forward leaks. Unlike disconnect, this pair is not wrapped in uninterruptible.

contracts.action: An existing managed server that does not answer now gets the 60s readiness budget, then the script exits 1 without replacing it
contracts.equivalent_path: The fresh-launch readiness wait (tunnel.ts:744) uses the same T3_READY_TIMEOUT_MS
contracts.before_after: Before: a 2s reuse probe, then kill and relaunch. After: up to 60s of wait_ready, then the error and exit, with ownership files kept.
contracts.visible_effect: The connection fails with 'Remote T3 server is still running but did not become ready' after about 60s.
contracts.failure_mode: Outer bound: the ssh launch command timeout is REMOTE_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 90s for the node runner and 900s for the archive runner (tunnel.ts:55, 65, 917-919). Worst-case inner sum: runtime-file resolve, a 2s reuse probe (line 676), 60s at line 720. That is about 62s, which fits under 90s. Each probe has a 1s per-call timeout (tunnel.ts:52, 875). A PID that is alive but not ours makes this fail permanently (see finding).

contracts.action: Treat a runtime file that names our own managed PID as our own server
contracts.before_after: REMOTE_PID comes from `$!` of nohup env run-t3.sh. The runner execs node or the t3 binary (tunnel.ts:458, 558), so the PID equals the server's process.pid that it writes to the runtime file. The port file is rewritten from the runtime file, then the managed branch at 711 checks liveness.
contracts.visible_effect: A reconnect keeps the managed server and no longer kills it as an external server.
contracts.failure_mode: resolve_default_runtime_port only checks kill -0 (tunnel.ts:650). server_running at 711 catches zombies but not a reused PID.

summary: The PR stops reconnects from killing the remote server. A stale forward is now closed without running the remote stop. The launch script recognises its own managed server through the default runtime file, skips re-probing a server it just adopted, ignores zombies, and when an existing managed server doesn't answer within 60s it fails instead of replacing it. The new shell-level tests run the real script against a fake server and cover these paths well. The main problem: any live PID that matches the pid/runtime files now counts as our busy server. That includes a PID reused after a reboot or crash, and in that case every reconnect fails after 60s and never recovers on its own. A smaller issue: the delete-then-close at line 1676 is not wrapped in uninterruptible the way disconnect's is.
